extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of American history and journalism; general readers interested in Revolutionary-era press
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and characterizing newspapers and printing practices in the American colonies during the Stamp Act–Revolutionary period (c.1765–1783), including partisan alignment, production tactics, circulation, and political influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political alignment (Patriot vs Loyalist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the paper openly supported the Patriot cause, the Royalist/Tory side, or attempted neutrality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly distinguishes 'Patriot papers' (e.g., Boston Gazette, Massachusetts Spy) from 'Tory papers' (e.g., Rivington’s Gazette, some New York papers). Alignment affected content (propaganda, attacks, defenses), audience reception, and survival (mob attacks, loss of patronage, suspensions). The chapter notes many degrees of Toryism and that papers not fully aligned with Patriots were generally considered Tory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial impartiality vs partisanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Normative claims about whether a newspaper should print both sides or take a partisan stance—especially in times of revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two views are presented: (1) the doctrine 'no press is free when it is under the control of one party'—a self-respecting paper should print both sides 'within reason and decency'; (2) the immediate revolutionary view that 'all who are not for us are against us' and neutrality is unacceptable. The guidance explains that during revolution there is 'little or no place for the former view' and impartial papers often suffered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the press as a political organ and mobilizer
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which a paper printed proceedings, town meetings, committee actions, letters, and other material that organized and promoted political resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: concerted publication of colonial legislatures' proceedings and town meetings protesting the Stamp Act; printing of non-importation agreements, blacklists, methods of enforcement; repeated advocacy of independence (e.g., Adams’ essays). The paper’s role in preparing public opinion and coordinating action is treated as a primary function during 1765–83.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactics to evade restrictive laws and censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical production and design methods newspapers used to avoid compliance with laws (e.g., Stamp Act) or to signal protest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods included issuing weekly numbers without serial numbering or imprint, sometimes without the regular nameplate (technically changing status to broadsides/handbills); using headings like 'No Stamped Paper to be had'; mourning make-up (black rules/tombstone front pages) to protest; suspending publication temporarily. These tactics are described as deliberate evasion and political protest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format, printing quality, and editorial content breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical and editorial quality: size, typography, foreign news, literary miscellany, local news quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rivington’s Gazetteer was praised for being 'one of the best' with 'a large, well-printed page, and excellent foreign news and literary miscellany' and 'local and colonial news ... brighter and better written.' Isaiah Thomas’s Spy changed format and frequency (triweekly → semiweekly → weekly) as it matured. Such production and content quality are used to assess a paper’s standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation and advertising patronage as measures of influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Subscription/circulation numbers and the strength of advertising revenue as indicators of a paper’s reach and success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Boston Gazette reached circulation of 2,000; Massachusetts Spy reached 3,500; Rivington claimed broad colonial and transatlantic distribution and 'good advertising patronage.' The text links circulation and advertising to influence and financial viability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship to political organizations and leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of connection between a paper and political clubs/figures (e.g., Caucus Club, Sons of Liberty, leading patriots) and the role of editors/contributors in political organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boston Gazette’s writers were 'in the main, the members of the Caucus Club' (Samuel Adams, John Adams, Joseph Warren, etc.), who 'cooked up paragraphs' and 'worked the political engine.' Such organizational ties are portrayed as central to editorial direction and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official printing contracts and government patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a paper did official printing for government and how such ties influenced editorial stance and economics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Post-Boy and News-Letter shops 'did official printing for the government and became intimately connected' and this relationship affected content and patronage. Official work could bind a paper to particular positions or revenue streams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to adapt continuity (suspension, relocation, resumption)
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper’s resilience measured by its use of suspension, relocation of presses, or resumption under changing military/political conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: Patriot presses removed from Boston at night (Gazette to Watertown, Spy to Worcester); New York papers publishing from Kingston, Poughkeepsie, Fishkill; suspensions during occupation and later resumption. The chapter treats adaptability as key to survival and continued influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk exposure and consequences for printers/editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent of personal danger, mob action, legal reprisals, imprisonment, financial ruin, or exile faced by printers/editors because of editorial positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: tax-collectors hanged in effigy; printers threatened with 'imminent Danger' to 'House, Person, and Effects'; Mein assaulted and fled to England; Rivington’s office mobbed and suspended; Gill arrested. The text uses these outcomes to show costs of partisanship and the fraught environment for editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pseudonyms, anonymous contributions, and propaganda techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices of publishing anonymous/pseudonymous political essays and coordinated pen-names to circulate arguments and manage authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Samuel Adams used at least a score of pen-names; Gazette contributors wrote over many pen-names, making authorship difficult to assign. The chapter links such anonymity to organized propaganda and editorial direction (e.g., coordinated pieces advocating independence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial policy statements and public positioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit publisher/editor statements about the paper’s mission (e.g., 'Open to all Parties', 'Ever Open and Uninfluenced Press') as rhetorical/strategic positioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the Massachusetts Spy motto 'Open to all Parties, but Influenced by None,' and Rivington’s claim his 'press has been open to publication from ALL PARTIES.' Such declarations functioned to attract contributors/readers or to justify positions, but actual practice often diverged and produced controversy.
